ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Clara Barton — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Primary care visit for low mood, exhaustion, and poor sleep after returning from a long humanitarian deployment

text.paragraph: Primary care visit for low mood, exhaustion, and poor sleep after returning from a long humanitarian deployment [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: Exhausted, low, and sleeping three or four hours a night since coming home; feels she is no use to anyone. [S]
Worried that stopping work would let down the families and staff who rely on her, and wonders whether she simply needs a long rest. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Clarissa Harlowe Barton was born on December 25, 1821, in North Oxford, Massachusetts, the youngest of five children. [D]
Her diary records a brief period of depression in the spring of 1852, while she was teaching in New Jersey; her biographer judged that the mood did not last long. [D]

From 1861 she supplied and tended wounded soldiers at battlefields and field hospitals through the Civil War; after working for several days following the Battle of Antietam in September 1862 she was weakened by typhoid fever. [D]
In her account of the eve of the Battle of Antietam she wrote that she was faint but could not eat, weary but could not sleep, and depressed but could not weep. [D]
From March 1865 to 1869 she ran an office that answered 63,182 letters and identified 22,000 missing soldiers. [D]

In December 1868 she lost her voice while giving a lecture, from fatigue and mental prostration; in her own later account, nervous prostration had declared itself and she lay helpless all winter in Washington. [D]
In September 1869, on her doctor's advice, she travelled to Europe to regain her health. [D]
During the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 and 1871 she organized civilian relief in Strasbourg, Paris, and other French cities. [D]

In 1872 and 1873 she suffered nervous exhaustion and temporarily lost her eyesight; in a letter she wrote that she broke down with a cough in England in October 1872 and was confined to bed for eight months. [D]

After her return in October 1873 she broke down again with what she called prostration of the nervous system, deepened by her only sister's death in May 1874; she wrote that for almost a year she averaged less than two hours of sleep a day and could not write her name for over four months. [D]
A 1995 review by Spiegel describes her long-term nervous prostration and argues that the therapy she received changed her behavioral approach to illness and to life. [R]
Her biographer Elizabeth Brown Pryor, as quoted in a 2012 newspaper article, describes a long struggle with depression that was lifted by a need for her services. [R]
Her mother died on July 18, 1851, and her father on March 21, 1862. [D]

text.paragraph: Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Small, upright, neatly dressed; speech soft and slow; good eye contact; cooperative and precise. Mood "worn out and no use to anyone"; affect constricted and tearful at times; thought process linear; no suicidal ideation, intent, or plan; no psychotic features; insight and judgment good. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

tr.td: Major depressive disorder, recurrent, moderate (moderately severe symptoms at intake), after a prolonged humanitarian deployment; synthetic modern diagnosis linked to her documented periods of depression and nervous prostration

S — Synthetic modern diagnosis. Her periods of depression and nervous prostration are documented in her own words (D); calling them major depression is a retrospective interpretation (R), and no diagnosis was made in her lifetime.
Occupational burnout after eighteen months leading field medical relief in a war zone
S — Synthetic contributing factor echoing her documented exhaustion after wartime relief work; burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a mental disorder.

list.item: Major depressive disorder, recurrent, moderate (moderately severe symptoms at intake), after a prolonged humanitarian deployment; synthetic modern diagnosis linked to her documented periods of depression and nervous prostration: active, confirmed [S]
Occupational burnout after eighteen months leading field medical relief in a war zone: active, confirmed [S]

Shared decision-making: combined psychotherapy and an antidepressant for a recurrent, moderately severe episode; she chose cognitive behavioral therapy and sertraline. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]

Start sertraline 50 mg each morning; check tolerability and safety at two weeks; increase to 100 mg if the PHQ-9 has fallen by less than 50 percent after four to six weeks. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]

Weekly cognitive behavioral therapy with the clinic psychologist, by video or in person, for about 16 sessions, including behavioral activation and insomnia components. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]

Collaborative safety plan with warning signs, coping steps, people to contact, the clinic number, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; medicines stored safely and dispensed in 30-day supplies. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024) [S]

Psychiatry consultation to confirm the diagnosis, exclude bipolar disorder and PTSD, and advise on treatment of a recurrent episode. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]

PHQ-9 at every visit and at least monthly until remission; suicide-risk review at every visit; continue sertraline for at least twelve months after remission because the episode is recurrent. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]

Burnout and work: two weeks of medical leave, then a phased return with a 45-hour cap, no field deployment for at least six months, delegation of the families' correspondence, and a peer support group for relief workers. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]

Sleep and activity: fixed wake time, no work after 8 pm, a daily 30-minute walk, regular meals, and limited alcohol; prolonged bed rest or withdrawal from activity is explained as unhelpful for depression. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]

Screen for bipolar disorder, PTSD, anxiety, and unhealthy alcohol use, and check thyroid, blood count, vitamin B12, and a metabolic panel for medical contributors to fatigue. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]
